clues.q: This part of speech names a person, place, thing or idea
This part of speech expresses an action like 'run' or 'jump' or a state of being like 'is'
This part of speech describes a noun, as 'blue' or 'happy' do
This curvy punctuation symbol ends a sentence like 'Are you okay'
This raised punctuation mark shows possession in 'Sam's dog' and replaces missing letters in 'don't'
This part of speech, like 'she', 'it' or 'they', takes the place of a noun
This soundalike of 'there' and 'their' is a contraction meaning 'they are'
The old spelling rhyme says 'I before E, except after' this letter
'Big' and 'large' are examples of these words with the same or nearly the same meaning
'Hot' and 'cold' are examples of these words with opposite meanings
This part of speech, like 'quickly' or 'very', often ends in -ly and modifies a verb or adjective
This two-word contraction is often confused with 'its', the possessive form
This punctuation mark, made of two dots stacked vertically, often introduces a list
Small joining words like 'and', 'but' and 'or' belong to this part of speech
Words like 'in', 'under' and 'between' that show how a noun relates to the rest of the sentence are this part of speech
This soundalike of 'to' and 'two' means 'also' or 'more than enough'
'Pair' and 'pear' are an example of these words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning
This punctuation mark, a dot over a comma, can join two closely related complete sentences
'Don't', 'can't' and 'I'm' are examples of this shortened form of two words
This part of speech, like 'wow', 'oops' or 'ouch', expresses sudden emotion
This group of words with its own subject and verb can stand alone as a complete sentence
Writing 'I love pizza, it is delicious' commits this error of joining two sentences with only a light punctuation mark
This -ing verb form acts as a noun, as 'swimming' does in 'Swimming is fun'
In 'The dog chased the ball', 'the ball' plays this role, receiving the action of the verb
'The cake was eaten by Sam' is written in this construction, which makes the receiver of the action the subject
Named after an English university, it's the optional punctuation mark before 'and' in 'red, white, and blue'
This verb usually means 'to influence', while its soundalike is usually a noun meaning 'a result'
Three dots in a row signal left-out words or a trailing thought; this is the name of the mark
'Buzz', 'sizzle' and 'kaboom' are examples of these words that imitate the sounds they describe
NASA, scuba and laser are examples of this kind of word, formed from initial letters and pronounced as a word
'Walking to school, the rain soaked my shoes' contains this error, where an opening phrase has nothing sensible to describe
This verb mood, used in 'If I were you' and 'I wish it were Friday', expresses wishes and hypotheticals
Grammar sticklers say a supermarket sign reading '10 items or less' should use this word instead
Longer than a hyphen, this punctuation mark is named after the width of a capital letter in old printing
Not to be confused with 'principle', this word names the head of a school
This part of a sentence tells something about the subject and always contains the main verb
Not to be confused with 'stationary', meaning not moving, this word means writing paper and envelopes
This structure has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause
This verb tense, as in 'I have eaten', combines 'have' or 'has' with a past participle
In 'I gave her the book', 'her' plays this role, naming who receives the book
This mark of two dots over a vowel, as in 'naïve', shows the vowel is pronounced separately from the one before
'To boldly go' is a famous example of this construction that puts a word between 'to' and its verb
This rare punctuation mark, ‽, combines a question mark and an exclamation point
Named for Mrs. Malaprop in Sheridan's 'The Rivals', it's the comic misuse of a soundalike word
In 'Tom, my older brother, is tall', 'my older brother' is this kind of noun phrase that renames the noun beside it
This term for a misheard phrase that still sort of makes sense, like 'for all intensive purposes', comes from someone writing 'acorn' oddly
This symbol's name comes from schoolchildren reciting '& per se and' at the end of the alphabet
The paragraph mark ¶ goes by this odd name
In 'a broken vase', 'broken' is this verb form, which also follows 'have' in perfect tenses
Using a plural-looking pronoun for one person, as in 'Someone left their umbrella', is known as this
